standard_text: Compare properties (rate of change and initial value) of two linear functions represented in different ways (algebraically, in a table, in a graph, or verbally).

progression.narrative:
This standard asks students to put two linear functions side by side -- when the two are handed to them in DIFFERENT forms -- and decide how their properties compare. Every linear function carries the same two properties no matter how it is written: a rate of change (slope) and an initial value (the y-intercept, also called the starting value). So the whole standard rests on one repeated move: pull the rate of change and the initial value out of whatever form a function is in -- an equation y = mx + b, a table of values, a graph, or a verbal description -- and then line the two functions' properties up against each other.

The arc begins by making the forms feel interchangeable: a student first learns to recognize the SAME function shown two ways, matching a table to its equation, so they trust that slope and intercept survive a change of form. Next they read the two properties out of a single graph or verbal description -- the forms that hide the numbers. Once a student can extract a rate of change and an initial value from any form, the comparison work starts: first comparing two functions given in the SAME form (two equations, two graphs), then the standard's true target -- comparing two functions given in DIFFERENT forms (an equation versus a table) and stating which grows faster or starts higher. From there they quantify the gap by computing the difference between the two rates of change, and at the top of the progression they build a brand-new representation engineered to have a greater or lesser slope and intercept than a given one. The through-line we keep naming: a linear function has exactly two comparable properties -- how fast it changes (rate of change/slope) and where it starts (initial value/y-intercept) -- and those two properties can be read out of any form.

steps.rationale: Recognize the same linear function across forms by matching a table to its equation. Equivalence must come before comparison so students trust that the slope and intercept are preserved when the form changes.
Read the rate of change and initial value out of a graph or verbal description -- the two forms that hide the numbers -- so both properties are in hand before any comparison.
Compare two functions given in the SAME form; the Approaching step where students first line up two rates of change and two intercepts and must stop using the intercept to judge growth.
The standard's core (At proficiency): compare two functions given in DIFFERENT forms -- an equation versus a table -- and state which grows faster or starts higher, computing the table's rate first.
Quantify the comparison by computing the difference between the two functions' rates of change, the numeric-response form of the At-proficiency task.
The Above-proficiency synthesis: build a new representation constrained to have a greater or lesser slope and intercept than a given function.

skills.name: Read the slope and y-intercept from an equation y = mx + b

prerequisite_skill.description: Given a linear equation in y = mx + b form, name the number that is the slope (rate of change) and the number that is the y-intercept (initial value).
prerequisite_skill.check_question: In y = 4x + 9, which number is the rate of change and which is the starting value?

skills.i_do_script: The reading rule has a reason: in y = 3x + 5, plug in x = 0 and only the 5 survives -- that's why the added-on number is the initial value (y-intercept). Step x up by 1 and y grows by exactly 3 -- that's why the number with x is the rate (slope). Position is the shortcut; the jobs are why it works. Every equation written as y = mx + b hands you the two properties directly: the number multiplied by x is the slope (rate of change) and the number added on is the y-intercept (initial value). Watch y = 3x + 5: the 3 is the slope because it multiplies x, and the 5 is the y-intercept because it is the amount added. So this function changes by 3 for each 1 of x and starts at 5 when x is 0.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the two numbers -- calls the added constant the slope and the coefficient of x the y-intercept
canonical_error.example: For y = 3x + 5, says the slope is 5 and the y-intercept is 3, reading the equation backwards
canonical_error.why: The student does not tie the slope to the number that MULTIPLIES x. The rate of change is always the coefficient of x; the initial value is the stand-alone constant. Swapping them reports the wrong property for each.

skills.item_template: A linear equation in y = mx + b form. Student names the slope and/or the y-intercept. Short-response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: In the equation y = 3x + 5, what is the slope (rate of change)?
In the equation y = 3x + 5, what is the y-intercept (initial value)?
What is the rate of change of y = -2x + 7?
What is the initial value (y-intercept) of y = 6x - 4?
In y = (1/2)x + 8, name the slope and the y-intercept.
sample_items.answer: slope 1/2; y-intercept 8

redirect_script.stop: Which number is multiplied by x?
redirect_script.prompt: Plug in x = 0: the survivor is the intercept. Step x up by 1: the growth is the slope. Point to the number sitting right next to the x -- that is the slope (rate of change). The number by itself, with no x, is the y-intercept (starting value). Label them before you compare anything.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the slope to the number times x and the y-intercept to the lone constant -- exactly right.

vocabulary.definition: The number that multiplies x in y = mx + b; how much y changes for each 1 that x changes.
The constant added in y = mx + b; the value of y when x is 0, also called the starting value.

next_steps.if_fail: Review slope-intercept form y = mx + b (7.AF.3).

Write 'y = 7x + 2. Name the slope and the y-intercept.'
Which number multiplies x, and which stands alone?
The 7 multiplies x, so the slope is 7. The 2 stands alone, so the y-intercept is 2.
If a student says the slope is 2, ask 'is 2 attached to an x?'
Your turn: for y = -5x + 3, name the slope and the y-intercept.

skills.name: Find the rate of change from a table (change in y over change in x)

prerequisite_skill.description: Given a table of values, compute the rate of change by dividing the change in y by the change in x.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A table has x = 0, 2, 4 and y = 1, 7, 13. What is the rate of change?

skills.i_do_script: When x skips from 0 straight to 2, a row is hidden -- so the jump you see in y is really two steps of climbing rolled into one, and the per-step rate means splitting that jump across the skipped steps. To find a table's rate of change, I pick two rows and divide the change in y by the change in x. Watch x = 0, 2, 4, 6 with y = 1, 7, 13, 19: from the first two rows y goes up 6 while x goes up 2, so the rate is 6 divided by 2 = 3. I must divide by the change in x -- if x jumps by 2, the 6 is NOT the rate by itself.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses the change in y as the rate without dividing by the change in x when x does not step by 1
canonical_error.example: For x = 0, 2, 4 and y = 1, 7, 13, says the rate is 6 (the change in y) instead of 6 / 2 = 3
canonical_error.why: The student assumes x always steps by 1, so 'the change in y' looks like the rate. When x steps by 2 or more, the rate is change in y DIVIDED by change in x -- skipping the division inflates the rate.

skills.item_template: A short table of (x, y) values with equal x-steps. Student computes the rate of change. Short-response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: A table has x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 4, 9, 14, 19. What is the rate of change?
A table has x = 0, 2, 4, 6 and y = 1, 7, 13, 19. What is the rate of change?
A table has x = 0, 5, 10 and y = 2, 12, 22. What is the rate of change?
A table has x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 3, 5, 7, 9. What is the rate of change?
A table has x = 0, 3, 6 and y = 10, 16, 22. What is the rate of change?

redirect_script.stop: How much did x change between those rows?
redirect_script.prompt: Look for the hidden rows first: how many skipped steps is that y-jump rolling together? Find the change in y AND the change in x, then divide: change in y over change in x. If x jumped by 2, don't stop at the change in y -- divide it by 2.
redirect_script.praise: You divided the change in y by the change in x -- that's the true rate of change.

vocabulary.definition: The change in y divided by the change in x between two rows of a table; the slope.
How much the x-value increases from one row to the next; the number you divide by.

next_steps.if_fail: Review computing unit rate and slope from a table (7.RP.2).

worked_example_script.text: Write a table: x = 0, 3, 6 and y = 4, 10, 16.
In the table x = 0, 3, 6 with y = 4, 10, 16, the rows x = 1 and x = 2 are hidden. y climbed 6 across those 3 steps -- how much per single step? Fill in the hidden y-values for x = 1 and x = 2.
How much does y change, and how much does x change, between the first two rows?
y goes up 6, x goes up 3, so the rate is 6 divided by 3 = 2.
If a student answers 6, ask 'did x go up by 1, or by 3?'
Your turn: x = 0, 2, 4 and y = 5, 9, 13 -- find the rate of change.

skills.name: Recognize the same linear function shown as an equation and as a table
skills.i_do_script: The same linear function can be written as an equation or as a table, and both must agree on the slope AND the y-intercept. Watch y = 2x + 5: at x = 0 y is 5, at x = 1 y is 7, at x = 2 y is 9 -- so the matching table is 5, 7, 9, 11. To check a table, I test EVERY row against y = 2x + 5, not just the first one. A table that starts at 5 but climbs by 1 each step is a different function, even though it shares the starting value.

canonical_error.pattern: Matches only the y-intercept (the value at x = 0) and ignores whether the rate of change also fits
canonical_error.example: For y = 2x + 5, picks the table 5, 6, 7, 8 because it starts at 5, ignoring that it rises by 1 each step instead of by 2
canonical_error.why: The student checks a single point -- usually the starting value -- and stops. Two representations are the same function only when BOTH the slope and the y-intercept match, so every row must satisfy the equation.

skills.item_template: A linear equation (or a table) and four candidate tables (or equations). Student selects the equivalent representation. MC.

redirect_script.stop: Does EVERY row fit, or just the first?
redirect_script.prompt: Test the rate of change AND the starting value. Plug in x = 0 to check the y-intercept, then check that each step climbs by the slope. A table is only the same function when both match.
redirect_script.praise: You checked both the starting value and the rate of change on every row -- that's a real match.

vocabulary.definition: Different forms (equation, table, graph, words) of the SAME function, agreeing on slope and y-intercept.
An (x, y) pair makes the equation true; every row of a matching table must satisfy it.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'Which table represents y = 4x + 1?' and a table 1, 5, 9, 13 for x = 0,1,2,3.

practice_problems.answer: Table: 6, 5, 4, 3. It does not represent y = x + 6 (that would climb, not fall) -- any equation with a positive slope fails.

skills.name: Extract the rate of change and initial value from a graph or verbal description
skills.i_do_script: A graph and a verbal description hide the two properties, so I dig them out. From a graph I read the y-intercept where the line crosses the y-axis, and the rate of change as how far up the line goes for each 1 across. Watch a line through (0, 4) and (2, 10): the initial value is 4 (at x = 0) and the rate of change is (10 - 4)/(2 - 0) = 3. In words, 'a pool holds 20 gallons and fills 5 gallons a minute' means initial value 20 and rate of change 5 -- the one-time amount is the start, the per-unit amount is the rate.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the one-time starting amount and the per-unit rate in a verbal description
canonical_error.example: For 'a $30 activation fee plus $15 per month,' says the rate of change is 30 and the initial value is 15, treating the fee as the rate
canonical_error.why: The student grabs numbers in the order they appear instead of by role. The starting amount happens once (initial value); the repeated per-unit amount is the rate of change. Reversing them mislabels both properties.

skills.name: Compare the rate of change and initial value of two functions in the same form
skills.i_do_script: To compare two linear functions shown the same way, I pull the rate of change and the initial value from EACH, then compare them separately -- and I never judge how fast a function grows by where it starts. Watch Function A: y = 2x + 9 and Function B: y = 5x + 3. Rates of change: A is 2, B is 5, so B grows faster. Initial values: A is 9, B is 3, so A starts higher. The trap is saying A grows faster because 9 is bigger -- but 9 is the starting value, not the rate.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges which function grows faster by the initial value (y-intercept) instead of the rate of change
canonical_error.example: For A: y = 2x + 9 and B: y = 5x + 3, says A grows faster because it starts higher (9 > 3), ignoring that B's rate of change 5 is greater than A's 2
canonical_error.why: The student uses the wrong property to answer a rate question. 'Grows faster' is decided only by the slope; the y-intercept tells you where a function starts, not how fast it climbs.

skills.name: Compare two functions given in different forms (equation versus table)
skills.i_do_script: This is the heart of the standard: two functions are handed to me in DIFFERENT forms, so I get each one's rate of change and initial value first, then compare. Watch Antonio's savings y = 25x + 350 (rate 25, start 350) against Paul's table 100, 130, 160, 190 for x = 0,1,2,3. Paul's rate is the climb, 30 per week, and his start is 100. So Antonio starts higher (350 > 100) but Paul grows faster (30 > 25). The trap is comparing Antonio's 25 to a raw number in Paul's table instead of computing Paul's rate of change.

canonical_error.pattern: Compares the equation's slope to a number read straight from the table instead of computing the table's rate of change
canonical_error.example: For y = 5x + 8 versus a table with y = 3, 9, 15, 21 at x = 0, 2, 4, 6, compares 5 to a table value like 9 (or uses the change in y, 6) instead of the table's true rate 3
canonical_error.why: The student never converts the table to its rate of change. A table's rate is change in y over change in x; grabbing a y-value or an undivided change makes the two functions un-comparable.

skills.item_template: One function as an equation and one as a table. Student selects the true comparison of rate of change and/or initial value. MC.

skills.name: Calculate the difference between the rates of change of two functions
skills.i_do_script: Two climbers can start at different heights AND climb at different speeds -- and 'how much faster' is a question about the speeds, not about the starting heights. Find each speed first; only then does subtracting mean anything. Sometimes the comparison must be a number: how much greater is one rate of change than the other? I find each function's rate of change first, then subtract. Watch Function J (table 2, 5, 8, 11 at x = 0,1,2,3) and Function K (table 1, 2, 3, 4 at x = 0,2,4,6). J's rate is 3; K climbs 1 while x climbs 2, so K's rate is 1/2. The difference is 3 - 1/2 = 5/2. I subtract the RATES, never the raw y-values.

canonical_error.pattern: Subtracts corresponding y-values or the initial values instead of first finding and then subtracting the two rates of change
canonical_error.example: For J (rate 3) and K with y-values 1, 2, 3, 4, subtracts a pair of y-values (or uses K's change 1) to get a difference like 2 instead of 3 - 1/2 = 5/2
canonical_error.why: The student subtracts before converting each table to a rate. The 'difference in rates of change' requires computing each slope first (change in y over change in x), then subtracting those slopes -- not the outputs.

vocabulary.definition: One function's rate of change minus the other's; found after computing each slope.

worked_example_script.text: Write both tables side by side for x = 0, 1, 2, 3: Climber J at heights 4, 7, 10, 13 and Climber K at heights 1, 3, 5, 7.
J starts 3 higher than K (4 vs 1) -- but is that a speed? How fast does each climber rise per step? And watch the gap between them: 3, then 4, then 5, then 6 -- what is the gap doing?

J climbs 3 per step and K climbs 2 per step, so the gap grows by exactly 1 each step -- that growing-by-1 IS the difference in their rates: 3 - 2 = 1. Subtracting the starting heights (4 - 1 = 3) only tells you the head start, and a head start never changes with time.
What is each table's rate of change?
J climbs 3 each step, so J's rate is 3. K climbs 2, so K's rate is 2. The difference is 3 - 2 = 1.
If a student subtracts 4 - 1 = 3 (the first y-values), ask 'is that a rate, or just one output?'
Your turn: J climbs by 5, K climbs by 2 -- what is the difference in their rates?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student subtracts corresponding y-values or initial values instead of the two rates of change.
misconception_redirects.say: Compute each table's rate of change first (change in y over change in x), write the two rates down, THEN subtract them. Never subtract the y-values in the tables.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found both rates of change and subtracted those -- that's the difference in rates.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reports the change in y as the rate when x does not step by 1.
misconception_redirects.say: Check the x-step. If x climbs by 2, divide the change in y by 2 before you compare.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided by the change in x, so your rate is correct.

quick_checks.prompt: J rate 4, K rate 1/2 -- difference in rates?
quick_checks.look_for: 7/2. An answer of 3 or 4 means the student didn't handle K's rate.

quick_checks.prompt: A table shows 1, 2, 3 at x = 0, 2, 4. What is its rate of change?
quick_checks.look_for: 1/2. An answer of 1 diagnoses using the undivided change.

K climbs ___ while x climbs ___, so K's rate is ___.

steps.annotation: J climbs 3 while x climbs 1.
K climbs 1 while x climbs 2 -- divide to get 1/2.
Subtract the two rates, not the y-values.
The rates of change differ by 5/2.

steps.annotation: Find J's rate of change.
Find K's rate of change.

State the difference in rates of change.

skills.name: Create a new representation with a greater or lesser slope and y-intercept
skills.i_do_script: At the top of this standard I build a NEW function to order: same rate but a bigger start, or a bigger rate but the same start. First I read the given function's two properties, then I change ONLY the property the prompt names. Watch Function G in a table 2, 6, 10 at x = 0, 3, 6: its rate of change is 4/3 and its y-intercept is 2. Asked for the same rate and a greater y-intercept, I keep 4/3 and pick any start above 2 -- for example y = (4/3)x + 5. I do NOT touch the slope, because only the intercept was supposed to change.

canonical_error.pattern: Changes the wrong property -- alters the one the prompt says to keep fixed
canonical_error.example: Asked for the SAME rate of change as G (slope 4) and a GREATER y-intercept, writes y = 6x + 2 (raised the slope, kept the intercept) instead of y = 4x + 5
canonical_error.why: The student edits whichever number is easiest rather than the one named. 'Same rate, greater intercept' means the slope must stay identical and only the constant may increase -- and vice versa.

skills.item_template: A given linear function (often a table). Student writes an equation whose slope and/or y-intercept meet a stated greater/lesser/same constraint. Extended response.

sample_items.stem: Function G is the table below. Write an equation for a function with the SAME rate of change as G and a GREATER y-intercept than G.
sample_items.answer: G has rate 4 and y-intercept -3, so any y = 4x + b with b > -3. Example: y = 4x + 2.

sample_items.stem: Function G is the table below. Write an equation for a function with the SAME rate of change as G and a GREATER y-intercept than G.
sample_items.answer: G has rate 4/3 and y-intercept 2, so any y = (4/3)x + b with b > 2. Example: y = (4/3)x + 5.

sample_items.stem: Function G is y = 2x + 5. Write an equation for a function with a GREATER rate of change than G and the SAME y-intercept.
sample_items.answer: Keep the intercept 5 and raise the slope above 2: any y = mx + 5 with m > 2. Example: y = 3x + 5.

sample_items.stem: Function G is the table below. Write an equation for a function with a LESSER rate of change than G and the SAME initial value.
sample_items.answer: G has rate 3 and initial value 4, so keep 4 and lower the slope below 3: any y = mx + 4 with m < 3. Example: y = 2x + 4.

sample_items.stem: Alex's trip cost is y = 0.10x + 5 (x = miles). Write an equation for Jamie whose cost per mile is MORE than Alex's and whose fixed cost is LESS than Alex's.
sample_items.answer: Slope above 0.10 and intercept between 0 and 5: any y = mx + b with m > 0.10 and 0 < b < 5. Example: y = 0.15x + 3.

redirect_script.stop: Which property is supposed to stay the same?
redirect_script.prompt: Underline the property the prompt says to keep (rate or intercept) and copy it EXACTLY. Change only the other one, up or down as asked. If you kept the slope, your slope should match G's slope.
redirect_script.praise: You held the fixed property steady and moved only the one the prompt named -- that's the constraint met.

vocabulary.definition: A rule your new function must satisfy, such as 'same rate of change, greater y-intercept.'
Many equations can satisfy the constraint (any b greater than G's), so more than one answer is correct.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for high school Algebra I (AI.L.3, AI.SEI.1) -- writing and comparing linear functions.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'G: y = 5x + 2. Write a function with a greater rate of change and the SAME y-intercept.'
Which property must stay the same, and which must change?
Keep the intercept 2 and raise the slope above 5, for example y = 8x + 2. Only the slope changed.
If a student writes y = 8x + 6, ask 'was the y-intercept supposed to stay the same?'
Your turn: G: y = 4x + 3. Write a function with the same rate of change and a LOWER y-intercept.

practice_problems.stem: Function G has slope 4. Give a slope that is greater than G's.
practice_problems.answer: Any number above 4 (e.g., 5).

practice_problems.stem: To keep the same rate of change as y = 3x + 1, what must the new equation's slope be?
practice_problems.answer: 3 (identical slope).

practice_problems.stem: Function G (table): -3, 1, 5, 9 at x = 0,1,2,3. Write an equation with the SAME rate of change and a GREATER y-intercept.
practice_problems.answer: G is y = 4x - 3; keep slope 4, raise intercept above -3: e.g., y = 4x + 2.

practice_problems.stem: Function G is y = 2x + 5. Write an equation with a GREATER rate of change and the SAME y-intercept.
practice_problems.answer: Keep intercept 5, raise slope above 2: e.g., y = 3x + 5.

practice_problems.stem: Tara answered a 'create a function' task. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: G: y = 4x - 3. Task: SAME rate of change, GREATER y-intercept.
practice_problems.answer: Tara changed the slope instead of the intercept. To keep the SAME rate of change she must keep slope 4; to get a GREATER y-intercept she raises -3, for example y = 4x + 2.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: edited the property that was supposed to stay fixed.

practice_problems.stem: Function G (table): 2, 6, 10 at x = 0,3,6. Write an equation with the SAME rate of change and a GREATER y-intercept.
practice_problems.answer: G is y = (4/3)x + 2; keep slope 4/3, raise intercept above 2: e.g., y = (4/3)x + 5.

practice_problems.stem: Alex: y = 0.10x + 5 (cost per mile 0.10, fixed cost 5). Write Jamie's equation with a HIGHER cost per mile and a LOWER fixed cost, and explain both choices.
practice_problems.answer: Any y = mx + b with m > 0.10 and 0 < b < 5, e.g., y = 0.15x + 3: 0.15 > 0.10 (higher per mile) and 3 < 5 (lower fixed cost).
practice_problems.notes: Two constraints at once (spec Alex/Jamie item).

practice_problems.stem: Given G: y = 5x + 4, write a function that GROWS FASTER but STARTS LOWER, then write one that GROWS SLOWER but STARTS HIGHER.
practice_problems.answer: Grows faster, starts lower: y = 8x + 1 (8 > 5, 1 < 4). Grows slower, starts higher: y = 2x + 9 (2 < 5, 9 > 4).
practice_problems.notes: Produce two functions with opposite trade-offs.

activities.title: Change the Right Number
activities.instructions:
1. Read the task: same rate of change as G (y = 4x - 3), greater y-intercept.
2. Read Tara's answer y = 6x - 3 and underline what she changed.
3. Write which property was supposed to stay the same.
4. Write a correct equation and explain why the slope must still be 4.

content.worked_problem: G: y = 4x - 3. Task: same rate, greater intercept. Tara wrote y = 6x - 3.
content.error_step: Tara raised the slope (4 to 6) and left the intercept alone.
content.why: 'Same rate of change' means the slope must stay 4; only the intercept may increase, e.g., y = 4x + 2.

activities.title: Meets the Constraint?
materials: Card set: one given function G plus 10 candidate equations
activities.instructions:
1. Post the target: G is y = 3x + 2; find functions with the SAME rate of change and a GREATER y-intercept.
2. Sort each candidate into 'Meets it' or 'Breaks it.'
3. For every 'breaks it' card, say which property is wrong (slope changed, or intercept not greater).
4. Debrief: how many correct answers exist, and what do they all share?

strategy_links.why: Editing the wrong property is a precise error a find-and-fix names by checking each constraint.
Writing why the slope must stay fixed builds the justification the Above-proficiency task expects.
Think-pair-share on 'how many correct answers exist?' surfaces the range-of-answers idea.
Gradual release from a fully worked constraint to an independent build supports the two-property version.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4 (compare two functions given in DIFFERENT forms) -- the standard's core and where the table-rate trap lives. If they pass, move up to S5 (quantify the difference in rates) and the S6 extension. If they fail, drop to S3 (compare two functions in the SAME form) and then S2 (extract rate and initial value from one graph/verbal representation). S1 (recognize equivalent forms) branches off as the below-grade equivalence check.
